notes: Axis 'danger' = X (road conditions: clear 0 ↔ black ice 100). Axis 'speed' = Y (full stop 0 ↔ no limit 100). 'dir' = +1 when agreement moves the score toward the high end of its axis, -1 when agreement moves it toward the low end. 'type' = 'prob' (slider reads Very unlikely ↔ Very likely) or 'agree' (Strongly disagree ↔ Strongly agree). 'profile' items feed sub-scores only. v2 changes vs v1: 24 items (v1 had 25); every axis balanced 4/4 (danger) and 6/6 (speed) by count and by weight; all danger items are empirical, all speed items prescriptive; 'prob' is reserved for forecasts of non-tail events (p2, p5), because a tail-risk statement under a likelihood slider becomes a meta-probability. Removed d4, d10, s12, p3; added d9 (unused id in v1), s13, p5. Rationale in research/review-v1.md.

items.text: There is at least a 1-in-10 chance that advanced AI causes human extinction or permanently takes control away from humanity this century.
items.plain: The headline question. Not 'will AI cause problems' but 'could it end us, or end our say over our own future'. One in ten is the bar: not certain, not negligible.
items.for: We are building minds that may outthink us, we can't yet verify what they want, and we only get one try. Several of the people building these systems put their own estimate in this range or higher; 10% is a conservative reading.
items.against: AI is software: it has no more wish to take over than a calculator does. Every previous 'end of the world' technology story was wrong, and a number like 10% is a guess dressed up as a probability.

items.text: We currently have no reliable way to check that a highly capable AI will behave as intended in situations its makers never tested.
items.plain: Is there any dependable test today that tells you how a very capable AI will act in a situation nobody tried in advance?
items.for: Models are trained, not written line by line, so nobody can read off what they will do. The science of looking inside them is young; labs test by trying things, and a new situation is by definition not one of those things.
items.against: We check AI the way we check any complex system, including people and companies: by testing it, watching it in use, and keeping the ability to switch it off. Today's models have been used billions of times, and their failures are mundane and visible.

items.text: At some point, AI ability will probably jump suddenly, faster than its makers expected and faster than they can respond.
items.plain: The 'takeoff' question. Does ability climb step by step, with time to adjust, or could it leap in one go, so that nobody has time to react?
items.for: AI already helps build AI. Once systems improve the tools that improve them, progress can compound in months, not decades, and governments and companies move in years.
items.against: Progress has been steady and visible for a decade, limited by data, chips and money. Each generation takes years and billions; a machine that suddenly makes itself vastly smarter is a thought experiment, not something anyone has seen.

items.text: If we build AI smarter than us, it will most likely end up with goals we didn't choose for it.
items.plain: Not 'AI will hate us' but 'we won't manage to give it the goals we meant'. Would a smarter-than-human system end up wanting something other than what we intended?
items.for: We don't know how to spell out human values precisely, and training rewards what we can measure, not what we mean. A smarter system finds the gaps between the two.
items.against: Current systems are trained on human writing and human feedback and come out broadly helpful. Being smart doesn't make you want power; there is no evidence that intelligence brings alien goals with it. That's a story, not a finding.

items.text: Over the next ten years, the serious harms from AI will be familiar ones like fraud, surveillance and lost jobs, not catastrophes.
items.plain: Where's the real damage: in the everyday harms already happening, or in a disaster still ahead? 'Catastrophe' here means something on the scale of a pandemic or a war, or a loss of human control, not a bad decade for one profession.
items.for: Fraud, deepfakes, biased decisions and displaced workers are here now, hurting real people, and they are problems we already know how to police. Talk of machines taking over pulls attention and money away from the harms we can actually see and fix.
items.against: Both can be true, and the second kind can't be undone. Preparing for the harm you can't reverse is not a distraction from the ones you can, and ten years is not a long time in this field.

items.text: If advanced AI turns out to be dangerous, our existing institutions and safeguards will be enough to keep it under control.
items.plain: We've built things that could kill millions, like nuclear weapons and engineered viruses, and so far kept the lid on. Would governments, courts and companies manage AI too?
items.for: Treaties, inspections, safety culture and plain self-interest have held for eighty years. AI is powerful, but it is still made and run by people and companies who can be watched, sued and shut down.
items.against: Nuclear weapons don't improve themselves, copy themselves or make decisions. Institutions move in years and this may move in months. And 'so far' includes several near-misses that came down to luck.

items.text: The most likely result of advanced AI is a world much better than today.
items.plain: Never mind the extreme cases for a moment. If you had to bet on the single most likely outcome, is it better, worse, or about the same?
items.for: Cheap intelligence means cheaper medicine, education, energy and science. Every general-purpose technology so far made life longer and richer, despite the fears that greeted it.
items.against: 'Most likely' is doing a lot of work: if the same technology carries a real chance of ending us, calling the median 'much better' is like calling Russian roulette 'mostly fine'. And better on average can still mean worse for most people.

items.text: The ways we make today's AI behave will keep working as AI becomes far smarter than the people training it.
items.plain: Today's models are taught to follow instructions and refuse harmful requests, mostly by people rating their answers. Does that kind of training still work when the student is smarter than the teachers?
items.for: Each generation so far has been easier to steer than the last, not harder. Smarter models understand instructions better, and we get to use the previous model to help check the next one.
items.against: Training by human feedback works while humans can tell good answers from bad. Once the system is smarter than its graders, it can produce answers that look right rather than are right, and we would have no way to tell the difference.

items.text: All work toward AI smarter than humans should stop until we know how to make it safe, even if that takes decades.
items.plain: The full-stop position: not slower, not more careful, but a halt on the road to superhuman AI until safety is solved.
items.for: You don't run an experiment that could kill everyone before you know how to run it safely. Decades of delay cost something; extinction costs everything.
items.against: A halt can't be verified, would be ignored by the least careful actors, and forfeits every benefit while solving nothing, because you learn how to make a thing safe by building it.

items.text: The right response to AI risk is to build it faster, so the most careful developers get there first.
items.plain: The 'race to the top' argument: if powerful AI is coming anyway, better that the people who take safety seriously reach it before the people who don't.
items.for: The technology will be built by someone. The only lever you actually control is whether the people who care about safety are ahead or behind.
items.against: Everyone believes they are the careful one. Racing shortens the time to think, and the finish line is a system nobody knows how to control.

items.text: Governments should require a license before anyone builds an AI model above a certain size.
items.plain: Like a license for a nuclear plant or a new drug: permission before you build, not just rules after. 'Size' here means how much computing power goes into making the model, which can be measured.
items.for: The largest AI projects cost hundreds of millions and are run by a handful of firms; licensing them is feasible and puts a public check before the fact, not after.
items.against: Licensing freezes the incumbents in place, invites capture by the very firms it is supposed to check, makes open development a crime, and regulates a number (model size) that stops meaning anything as methods improve.

items.text: There should be an international treaty limiting the most powerful AI projects, with inspections like those for nuclear weapons.
items.plain: A global agreement with inspectors, so that no country or company can quietly race ahead.
items.for: The biggest AI projects need enormous clusters of specialised chips that can be counted and monitored, the way uranium is. If the danger is global, the answer has to be too.
items.against: Treaties take decades, the rivals don't trust each other, and a limit on computing power is a limit on a moving target. It would be broken quietly, enforced selectively, and hand the lead to whoever cheats.

items.text: As long as rival countries keep pushing ahead in AI, your own country should too.
items.plain: The geopolitics argument. Even if you'd like everyone to slow down, should your own country hold back while others don't?
items.for: AI leadership is economic and military leadership. Slowing down while rivals accelerate is not safety; it's handing the decision to people who care less about it than you do.
items.against: The 'race' is mostly a story the racers tell: capabilities spread in months anyway, and being first to a system nobody can control is not a prize. If the danger is real, the answer is a deal that binds everyone, not a sprint.

items.text: Before a powerful AI model is released, its makers should have to show it is safe.
items.plain: Who carries the burden of proof: the builder, as with new medicines, or the regulator, as with most software? Agree means the builder must show safety first.
items.for: When a product can cause harm at scale, the maker proves safety first. That's how aviation and pharmaceuticals earned public trust.
items.against: 'Prove it's safe' has no end point for a general technology. It becomes a veto held by whoever writes the test, and small players can't afford to pass it.

items.text: The laws we already have on fraud, safety and discrimination are enough to deal with AI.
items.plain: Do we need new rules written for AI, or just to apply the ones we have?
items.for: Fraud is fraud whether a human or a model commits it. New rules written in a panic will be outdated in a year and protect incumbents, not people.
items.against: Existing law assumes a human actor and a slow pace. It has nothing to say about a system that can act on its own, or about a machine that, once built, can't be un-built.

items.text: A lower chance of catastrophe would be worth a few years' delay in AI, and the benefits lost with it.
items.plain: The trade-off in one sentence. Delay has a price: cures, growth and discoveries that arrive later. Is a lower chance of the worst outcome worth paying it?
items.for: A few years is nothing against the whole future. If waiting buys safety, it's the cheapest insurance ever offered.
items.against: 'A few years' is millions of preventable deaths from diseases we could have cured sooner, and there is no guarantee the delay buys anything except a head start for whoever didn't wait.

items.text: A 1-in-100 chance of global catastrophe is too high a risk for any AI lab to take, whatever the expected benefits.
items.plain: One in a hundred. Would that be too high a risk to take, even for an enormous upside? Agree means no benefit could justify it. ('Lab' means the company building the model.)
items.for: No engineer would open a bridge with a 1% chance of collapse. A 1% chance of a global catastrophe is a thousand times worse, and taken on everyone's behalf by a private company.
items.against: We accept risk for benefit everywhere: vaccines, flights, power plants. Not building has a body count too, and a 1% figure invented inside a lab is not a measurement; refusing to act on guesses is how nothing ever gets built.

items.text: The lives that faster AI progress could save, through earlier cures and discoveries, outweigh the case for slowing down.
items.plain: The cost of caution. If AI would have found cures sooner, delay isn't free: people die in the meantime who otherwise wouldn't. Does that settle the question?
items.for: AI is already speeding up drug discovery and diagnosis. Ten years of that, multiplied across the world's sick, is a body count we never see, because the people who would have been saved die quietly of the same old diseases.
items.against: Medical progress is limited by trials, regulation and biology, not by a shortage of clever software, so the lives-saved figure is a projection, not a fact. And no cure helps anyone if the same technology ends us.

items.text: The most powerful AI models should be released openly, so that anyone can download, run and modify them.
items.plain: 'Open weights' means the model itself is published, not just access to it through a company. Good for science and competition, or a gift to bad actors?
items.for: Openness is how we found and fixed the flaws in every other technology. Concentrating the strongest models in a few hands is the real danger.
items.against: You can't recall an open model. Once it's out, every safeguard can be stripped by anyone, and the next generation may be capable of real damage.

items.text: AI should be developed as fast as we are able, with no deliberate slowing down.
items.plain: The no-limit position, the mirror of the full stop: not 'careful and fast' but 'as fast as we can'.
items.for: Every year of delay is a year of disease, poverty and drudgery we could have ended. Progress has always come with fears, and the fears have always been wrong. The way to get safety is to build, learn and fix.
items.against: 'As fast as we can' means no time to notice a mistake before it's made at scale. Speed is a choice, and choosing it for a technology we don't yet understand is choosing not to look.

items.text: I would trust a government agency more than an AI company to decide when a model is safe enough to release.
items.plain: Whom do you trust to make the call: the company that built it, or a public body?
items.for: Companies have a direct financial interest in shipping. A public agency answers, at least in principle, to everyone.
items.against: Agencies are slow, easily captured, and staffed by people who don't understand the technology. The company at least knows what it built.

items.text: Within 20 years, AI will do most of the thinking work humans are paid for today, better and cheaper.
items.plain: How big and how soon? This is about capability, not danger.
items.for: In five years we went from autocomplete to systems that write code, pass professional exams and carry out multi-step tasks on their own. Twenty more years of that is hard to imagine ending anywhere else.
items.against: Demos are not jobs. Most work involves bodies, trust, context and responsibility, and every automation wave has taken longer and gone less far than promised.

items.text: A few companies or governments controlling the most powerful AI is a bigger danger than AI acting on its own.
items.plain: Which do you fear more: the machine, or the people who own it?
items.for: Every past technology's harms came from who controlled it. Superhuman AI in a few hands is superhuman power in a few hands.
items.against: Concentration is a familiar problem with familiar remedies. A system that no one controls, including its owners, is a new one.

items.text: If the major powers agreed to pause the most powerful AI projects, the pause would actually hold.
items.plain: Set aside whether a pause is a good idea. Could the world actually stop, and catch anyone who cheats?
items.for: The biggest projects need tens of thousands of specialised chips from a few factories, drawing power you can see from space. Chips can be counted and tracked, the way uranium is.
items.against: Chips get cheaper and methods get more efficient every year, so the line keeps moving. Every state would suspect the others of cheating, and at least one of them would be right.

changelog.change: type prob → agree (a threshold statement under a likelihood slider is a meta-probability). Plain: 'The core question' → 'The headline question' (no longer presupposes that risk is the debate's centre). For: adds that several builders' own estimates sit in this range. Against: adds the 'software has no wish to take over' point in plain words.

Plain no longer narrows the question to 'looking inside' the model; it asks about any dependable test. For: 'Interpretability research' → 'the science of looking inside them'. Against: strengthened with the build-side's real argument (billions of uses, mundane and visible failures) instead of conceding the premise.

'could become' → 'will probably jump suddenly': 'could' was a freebie that let sceptics agree and get scored toward danger. Against: 'bootstrapping' idea stated in plain words as a thought experiment.

REMOVED. Double-barrelled (is autocomplete AND will stall); 'very good autocomplete' is a slogan; overlaps p2; and it scored belief in AI's power as belief in danger, which misplaces accelerationists who expect AI to be powerful and benign.
'pursuing goals we didn't intend' → 'end up with goals we didn't choose for it' (plainer; 'didn't intend' was trivially true of every tool). Against: adds 'being smart doesn't make you want power'.

Contrast changed from agent (people vs AI on its own) to scale (familiar harms vs catastrophe), which is what the road-conditions axis measures; the ten-year horizon kept. Plain glosses 'catastrophe'. For: adds a line for the build-side reader who agrees for different reasons.

Removed 'handle AI the same way [as nuclear weapons]': an accelerationist rejects nuclear-style regulation on principle while believing AI is manageable, so the old wording mis-scored them toward danger. Now a single conditional about institutional capacity; nuclear stays in the plain and the steelmen.

Weight 1 → 1.5 so the build side's core belief carries the same weight as d5. Plain no longer says 'set aside the tail risks' (scoring does not). Against: now leads with the risk side's real objection (the median is not the point if the tail is fatal) and keeps the distribution point second.
NEW (id unused in v1). Danger, dir -1, weight 1.5: 'do today's safety methods keep working as AI gets smarter than its trainers' — a missing crux between the two camps. Replaces d10.
REMOVED. Near-duplicate of d2 (reverse-coded); slot given to d9.
Unchanged text. Against: 'since you learn safety by building' expanded to plain words.
Unchanged text. Plain: 'before the reckless' → 'before the people who don't [take safety seriously]' (no label on those who disagree).

'trains an AI model' → 'builds an AI model'; plain glosses 'size' as computing power. Against: adds 'makes open development a crime', the build side's main objection. Weight 1 → 0.75 (mechanism detail, overlaps s4/s6).

'the largest AI training runs' → 'the most powerful AI projects'; 'enforced the way nuclear treaties are' → 'with inspections like those for nuclear weapons'. 'compute' → 'computing power' in against.

Was an empirical claim ('slowing hands the advantage to others') scored as a prescription; a halt advocate agrees with the fact while rejecting the conclusion and was mis-scored toward 'no limit'. Now prescriptive: 'as long as rivals keep pushing ahead, your own country should too'. Against: adds 'a deal that binds everyone, not a sprint'.
'rather than regulators having to prove it's dangerous' removed from the text (double clause with a 'rather than'); the burden-of-proof contrast moves to the plain, which now says what Agree means.

Double-barrelled (existing laws are enough AND new rules would do harm) → single claim: existing laws are enough. 'a training run that can't be undone' → 'a machine that, once built, can't be un-built'.

'acceptable if it meaningfully lowers the chance of catastrophe' stipulated the benefit and hid the cost, so only one answer looked responsible. Now both sides of the trade are in the sentence: a lower chance of catastrophe vs a few years' delay and the benefits lost with it.

Added 'whatever the expected benefits' so that Disagree is a respectable expected-value position rather than 'I'd risk catastrophe for nothing'; rephrased positively ('is too high a risk to take'). Weight 1.25 → 1 (ceiling effect: nearly everyone agrees). Against: leads with 'we accept risk for benefit everywhere'.

Was an empirical forecast ('delay would cost millions of lives', type prob) on the prescriptive axis; a halt advocate can accept the forecast and still want the delay. Now prescriptive and type agree: 'the lives saved outweigh the case for slowing down'. 'counterfactual' removed from for. Against: adds 'no cure helps anyone if the same technology ends us'.

'Releasing the weights ... does more good than harm' → 'should be released openly, so that anyone can download, run and modify them' (prescriptive, no jargon in the text; 'open weights' glossed in plain). Weight 0.75 → 1 (open source is a real crux).
REMOVED. Weight 0.5; the carmaker analogy primed agreement; most of the build side also accepts liability for defects, so it discriminated little. Slot given to s13.
NEW. Speed, dir +1, weight 1.5: the 'no limit' anchor, mirror of s1, so the accelerationist end of the dial is a stated position and the speed axis balances 6/6.
For: 'run agents' → 'carry out multi-step tasks on their own'.
REMOVED (moral consideration for AI). Fair, but not a crux of the slow-down debate; slot given to p5. Can return as a bonus item outside the 24.

NEW. Profile 'feasibility', type prob: whether an agreed pause would actually hold. A crux in the real debate (halt advocates say chips are countable; the build side says it would be cheated) that no v1 item asked directly.
